newsitem.title: BELGIUM: Commission report criticises calf early marketing scheme.
newsitem.headline: Commission report criticises calf early marketing scheme.

text.p: The European Commission said in a report adopted on Friday that although an early marketing scheme for calves had done little to cut red meat production, it should be judged over a longer period.
Bu a calf-processing scheme, the so-called Herod premium, had proved to be very efficient and cost-effective, it added.

"While it's too early to draw any firm conclusions, the indications so far are that the early marketing premium is making very little contribution to reducing production," Commission agriculture spokesman Gerard Kiely said.
He added that the calf processing scheme was an efficient way of reducing production and working well, but unfortunately was only being applied in Britain, France, Portugal and Ireland.

The two schemes were approved by EU farm ministers last October in a bid to reduce production and help bring it into line with reduced demand following a scare that mad cow disease could be transmitted to humans.

The report is due to be discussed by EU farm ministers in Luxembourg on Monday. France last month criticised the early marketing scheme, saying it was encouraging imports of cheap Dutch veal and undermining the French market.
The report dismisses a complaint by France that the application of national weight limits distorted trade.

There is no statistical evidence to support the French claim that so-called "premium subsidised imports" were responible for low veal prices at the beginning of 1997, it said, adding that veal prices in the Netherlands historically been lower than in France.
The report suggested that the scheme may "simply constitute a production subsidy" and may have to be suspended to safeguard EU finances.
More than two million calves, or double the 1997 estimate, need to be covered by the scheme to make it cost effective, the report said.
The report urged more member states to use the calf processing scheme, saying it was by far the most efficient measure to cut production.

Up to the end of March some 330,000 calves had been slaughtered under the scheme with Britain accounting for 50 per cent. The estimated total cost of the scheme covering the slaughter of one million calves would be 125 million ecus but with savings in terms of lower production and intervention amounting to 690 million ecus. REUTER
